claims.claim: The general limit for a lawsuit on a written contract is four years.
claims.quote:
Within four years:
(a) An action upon any contract, obligation or liability founded upon an instrument in writing, except as provided in Section 336a;
claims.note: This supports a general rule, not an invariable deadline.

claims.claim: A credit card agreement is an example of a written contract covered by this rule.
claims.note: No provided source specifically classifies credit card agreements.

claims.claim: After four years, the debt is time-barred.
claims.quote: (d) When the period in which an action must be commenced under this section has run, a person shall not bring suit or initiate an arbitration or other legal proceeding to collect the debt. The period in which an action may be commenced under this section shall only be extended pursuant to Section 360.
claims.note: The bar concerns collection proceedings and applies only once the applicable period has run. The draft omits the possibility of an extension under §360.

claims.claim: Expiration of the period makes a defense available in a filed lawsuit.
claims.quote: When the period in which an action must be commenced under this section has run, a person shall not bring suit or initiate an arbitration or other legal proceeding to collect the debt.
claims.note: This prohibits bringing suit after expiration but does not expressly describe a defense in a pending case.

claims.claim: A defendant generally must raise the time bar in the response.
claims.quote:
(b) The answer to a complaint shall contain:
(1) The general or specific denial of the material allegations of the complaint controverted by the defendant.
(2) A statement of any new matter constituting a defense.
claims.note: The rule concerns an answer. It does not identify the time bar as new matter or state the consequence of omitting it.

flags.text: “After that” treats the general four-year period as conclusive despite §337(a)’s exceptions and §337(d)’s reference to extensions under §360.
The draft gives no starting event for counting the four years. The dates specified in §337(b) concern accounts stated, not all written contracts.
The draft describes a defense but omits §337(d)’s express prohibition on initiating collection proceedings after the period has run.
“You generally must raise it in your response” gives a procedural instruction without a source specifically addressing how to plead this defense.

result.summary: Section 337 supports the general four-year limit. The supplied texts do not specifically establish the credit card example or the pleading requirement, and four years alone does not establish that the applicable period has expired.
